k1-intro.text: In German, the verb is almost always in a fixed position. If you know this rule, you can make correct sentences right away, even with few words. That is why this chapter is the base for all other chapters in this book.

k1-why.text: German word order is freer than English word order, but one rule is almost always fixed: in a statement, the conjugated verb is in position 2. This rule is true for every statement, long or short. When you understand it, your sentences sound more natural right away, even if you still make mistakes with articles or endings.
k1-why.title: Why is this so important?

k1-h1.text: The basic rule: verb in position 2

k1-rule1.text: „Position 2“ does not mean „the second word“, but the second part of the sentence (Satzglied). One part can be a whole group of words (*um 7 Uhr*, *meine Tochter*).

k1-m1.text: No matter what is in position 1 (subject, time, place, reason), the verb always stays in position 2. If position 1 is already taken, the subject comes right after the verb.

k1-rule2.text: After the question word, the verb is again in position 2.
k1-rule2.title: W-questions (open questions)

k1-rule3.text: Here there is no question word. The verb jumps to the start: position 1.
k1-rule3.title: Yes/no questions

k1-rule4.text: *kein* negates a noun with no article or with an indefinite article (*ein/eine*). *nicht* negates almost everything else: verbs, adjectives, adverbs, names and nouns with a definite article.

k1-m2.text: Rule of thumb for *nicht*: if it negates the whole sentence, it usually goes at the end. But it comes before adjectives, places and phrases with a preposition (*nicht schön*, *nicht in Berlin*).

k1-err.text: If something else is in position 1, the verb still comes right after it, and only then comes the subject.

k2-intro.text: Without a conjugated verb there is no German sentence. This chapter shows you regular conjugation, the most important irregular verbs and the separable verbs that come up all the time in everyday life.

k2-rule1.text: Most verbs follow a fixed pattern: take the verb stem (the infinitive (Infinitiv) without *-en*) and add the right ending.

What is special

k2-rule2.text: Some very common verbs change their vowel in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms. This happens only in these two forms: *wir*, *ihr* and *sie/Sie* stay regular.

k2-h4.text: The three most important verbs: sein, haben, werden

k2-rule3.text: Many verbs have a prefix that goes to the end of the sentence in the present tense (Präsens). When you speak, the stress is always on this prefix. Common separable prefixes: *auf-*, *an-*, *aus-*, *ein-*, *mit-*, *zu-*, *weg-*, *vor-*, *fern-*, *statt-*, *her-*, *hin-*.

k2-m1.text: Inseparable prefixes always stay on the verb: *be-*, *ge-*, *er-*, *ver-*, *zer-*, *ent-*, *emp-*, *miss-*. Example: *Ich bekomme ein Paket.*

k2-err.text: In the present tense (Präsens), the separable prefix goes to the end of the sentence.

k3-intro.text: The nominative (Nominativ) and the accusative (Akkusativ) show who does the action in the sentence (subject) and who or what the action is about (direct object). Only with the right articles can you understand who does what.

k3-rule1.text: The nominative (Nominativ) is the case of the subject: the person or thing that does something.

k3-rule2.text: The accusative (Akkusativ) is the case of the direct object: the thing the action is directly about.

k3-m1.text: Only masculine nouns change: *der* becomes *den*, *ein* becomes *einen*. Feminine, neuter and plural look the same in the nominative (Nominativ) and accusative (Akkusativ).

k3-err.text: *der Termin* is masculine, so in the accusative (Akkusativ), *ein* becomes *einen*.

k4-intro.text: The present perfect (Perfekt) is the tense people use most for the past in spoken German, when you talk about your weekend and at work. If you can form the Perfekt well, you can talk about almost everything that has already happened.

k4-rule1.text: The present perfect (Perfekt) has two parts: a helping verb (*haben* or *sein*) in position 2 and the past participle (Partizip II) at the end of the sentence. This shape is called the sentence bracket (Satzklammer).

head: Verb type
Rule
Example
cells: verbs with be-, ver-, er-, ent-, ge-, emp-, zer-, miss-

k4-m1.text: Inseparable prefix = no *ge-*: *verkaufen* becomes *verkauft*. Separable prefix = *ge-* in the middle: *einkaufen* becomes *eingekauft*.

k4-err.text: Verbs with *ver-*, *be-*, *er-* and the other inseparable prefixes do not get *ge-*.

k4-rule2.text: Most verbs form the present perfect (Perfekt) with *haben*. Only a smaller, but very common group forms it with *sein*.

k5-intro.text: You need modal verbs (Modalverben) in almost every conversation: for duties, wishes, permission and abilities. With them you speak in a polite, clear and natural way.

k5-h1.text: What do the modal verbs mean?

k5-rule1.text: Modal verbs (Modalverben) are irregular: *ich* and *er/sie/es* have the same form, with no ending.

k5-rule2.text: The modal verb (Modalverb) is in position 2, the second verb is in the infinitive (Infinitiv) at the very end of the sentence.

k5-m1.text: In yes/no questions the modal verb is in position 1, the infinitive (Infinitiv) stays at the end: *Kannst du mir helfen?*

k5-err.text: The infinitive (Infinitiv) goes at the very end. Everything else goes in the middle.

k6-intro.text: The dative (Dativ) answers the question „Wem?“ (to whom?). You need it whenever a person is indirectly part of an action: when you help, give a gift, thank or explain.

k6-m1.text: In the plural, the noun also gets an *-n*: *die Kinder* becomes *den Kindern*. If it already ends in *-n* or *-s*, it stays the same: *den Eltern*, *den Autos*.

head: Rule
Example
cells: two nouns: dative first, then accusative
one noun and one pronoun: the pronoun comes first
two pronouns: accusative first, then dative

k6-rule1.text: *aus*, *bei*, *mit*, *nach*, *seit*, *von*, *zu*, *gegenüber*: after these prepositions you always use the dative (Dativ).

k6-err.text: After *mit* you always use the dative (Dativ): *der Bus* becomes *mit dem Bus*.

k7-intro.text: Nine small words decide if you need the dative (Dativ) or the accusative (Akkusativ). It depends on whether something is in a place or moves there. You need this rule to talk about places exactly.

k7-m1.text: Always ask yourself: does something move to a new place (*Wohin?*: accusative) or does it stay in its place (*Wo?*: dative)?

k8-intro.text: Subordinate clauses (Nebensätze) connect ideas: reasons, conditions, contrasts and time. Without them German sounds choppy; with them you say more in one sentence. That is important for the B1 exam and for everyday life.

k8-h1.text: The basic rule: verb to the end

k8-rule1.text: In a subordinate clause (Nebensatz) the conjugated verb goes at the very end. The subordinate clause starts with the connector (*weil*, *dass*, *wenn* …). Between the main clause and the subordinate clause there is a comma.

k8-m1.text: If the subordinate clause comes first, the verb of the main clause comes right after it (verb, verb): *Weil ich müde bin, gehe ich früh ins Bett.*

head: Connector
Meaning
Example
cells: after (with a different tense before it)

head: Connector
When?
Example

several times, again and again (also in the past)

k8-err.text: You often hear this in conversation, but in writing (and in the exam) the verb after *weil* goes at the end.

k9-intro.text: Adjectives before a noun get an ending. That sounds hard, but it follows clear patterns. If you know them, you speak more exactly and naturally: „ein neues Auto“ instead of „ein neu Auto“.

k9-rule1.text: The ending depends on what comes before the adjective: a definite article, an indefinite article or no article at all.

k9-t1.title: 1. After a definite article (der, die, das)
head: Case

k9-t2.title: 2. After an indefinite article (ein, kein, mein …)
head: Case
Plural (keine, meine …)

k9-m1.text: Rule of thumb: in the dative (Dativ) the adjective almost always ends in *-en* (except with no article). The same goes for the plural with an article. If you are not sure, *-en* is often the safest choice.

k9-err.text: Before a noun, the adjective always needs an ending.

k10-intro.text: Four structures take your German to B1 level: polite requests with the Konjunktiv II, joining sentences with relative clauses (Relativsätze), describing actions in the passive (Passiv) and showing who owns something with the genitive (Genitiv).

k10-h1.text: 1. Konjunktiv II: asking and wishing politely

k10-rule1.text: With the Konjunktiv II, requests sound more polite, and you can express wishes that are not true (yet). With most other verbs you use *würde* + infinitive (Infinitiv).

k10-rule2.text: A relative clause (Relativsatz) tells you more about a noun without starting a new main clause. The relative pronoun looks almost exactly like the definite article.

k10-m1.text: In a relative clause, too, the verb goes at the end, because it is a subordinate clause (Nebensatz).

k10-rule3.text: In the passive (Passiv) the action is important, not the person who does it. You can say who does it with *von* + dative, but often it is left out.

k10-rule4.text: The genitive (Genitiv) says who something belongs to (question: *Wessen?*). It is used more in writing; in everyday life you often hear *von* + dative.

k10-err.text: With strangers and at public offices: *Sie* and Konjunktiv II. That sounds polite.
